title: At Ease in Gilbertese
bodyHtml:
The Gilbertese language is spoken by most of the over 100,000 people who live in the Pacific island nation of Kiribati. Here are some sentences in Gilbertese with their English translations:

GilberteseEnglish
ko nakonako ŋkoeYou are walking.
e nakonako te aiineA woman is walking.
i takaakaro ŋaiI am playing.
e nakonako nakon te titooa MeeriMary is walking to the store.
a tekateka irarikin taian auti taian aiineThe women are sitting next to the houses.
a tebotebo taian nakekei n te bong aeiThe people are bathing today.
i tebotebo inanon te auti ŋaiI am bathing in the house.
a takaakaro inanon te titooa taian ataeiThe children are playing in the store.
ko tekateka ŋkoe ningaabongYou will sit tomorrow.
a takaakaro irarikin te kawai taian ataei n te bong aeiThe children are playing next to the road today.

Answer the following questions in the Answer Sheets:

A1. Below are some Gilbertese sentences with their words in scrambled order:

  1. bong n Meeri auti e nakon te te nakonako aei
  2. inanon ŋai kawai i te tekateka
  3. ataei a nakon taian ningaabong kawai nakonako te

For each of these three sentences:

  1. Rearrange the words in the sentence into the correct Gilbertese word order.
  2. Translate the rearranged sentence into English.

A2. Translate into Gilbertese:

  1. The women will play tomorrow.
  2. You are sitting next to the store today.

hints.text: Look at the very first word of every Gilbertese sentence in the table: it is always one of i, ko, e or a. Compare those with who the subject is in the English translation (I, you, one person or thing, several people or things).

Every sentence in the table uses the same fixed sequence of slots, and each slot may be empty. In order the slots are: the little person word, the verb, any phrase saying where (nakon, inanon, irarikin plus a noun phrase), then the pronoun or noun that names the subject, then finally the time expression. Also work out which small word marks a singular noun and which marks a plural noun, and which time expression means today and which means tomorrow.

Try the method on a table sentence first. In "a takaakaro irarikin te kawai taian ataei n te bong aei" the slots are: a (subject is third person plural), takaakaro (the verb, playing), irarikin te kawai (next to the road), taian ataei (the children), n te bong aei (today). Notice that the subject noun phrase comes AFTER the where-phrase, and that te marks one road while taian marks more than one child. Now scramble-solve your own sentences by filling the same five slots.

explanationHtml:
What kind of puzzle is this?

You are given ten Gilbertese sentences with English translations. Nothing is hidden: every Gilbertese word appears often enough that you can match it to an English meaning, and the real work is figuring out the order in which Gilbertese lines its words up. That order is what lets you unscramble the sentences in A1 and build new ones in A2.

Step 1: the little word at the front

Every sentence begins with i, ko, e or a. Compare:

  • i takaakaro ŋai = "I am playing" — the subject is I
  • ko nakonako ŋkoe = "You are walking" — the subject is you
  • e nakonako te aiine = "A woman is walking" — one other person
  • a tebotebo taian nakekei n te bong aei = "The people are bathing today" — several other people

So this word is a person marker: a small grammatical word that agrees with the subject. i = 1st person singular, ko = 2nd person singular, e = 3rd person singular, a = 3rd person plural. Notice the marker is there even when the subject is also spelled out (e ... te aiine), so the marker is not itself the subject.

Step 2: the verbs and the pronouns

Right after the marker comes the verb: nakonako "walk", takaakaro "play", tekateka "sit", tebotebo "bathe". Independent pronouns are separate words: ŋai "I/me", ŋkoe "you".

Step 3: nouns, singular and plural

Compare te auti "the house" with taian auti "the houses", and te aiine with taian aiine "the women". So te goes with one thing and taian with more than one; the noun itself does not change shape. Nouns you can collect: auti house, titooa store, kawai road, aiine woman, ataei child, nakekei person.

Step 4: place words and time words

Three words introduce a place phrase: nakon "to", inanon "in(side)", irarikin "next to". Each is followed by its noun phrase, e.g. irarikin te kawai "next to the road".

Two time expressions show up: n te bong aei "today" (literally something like "on this day") and ningaabong "tomorrow". And here is the neat bit: ko tekateka ŋkoe ningaabong is translated "You will sit tomorrow" while a tebotebo taian nakekei n te bong aei is "The people are bathing today". The verb form never changes — English future versus present is only coming from the time word.

Step 5: the word order template

Line the sentences up and every one fits this sequence, with any slot allowed to be empty:

12345
person markerverbprepositional (place) phrasepronoun / noun subjecttime phrase

Check it against the longest example: a | takaakaro | irarikin te kawai | taian ataei | n te bong aei = "The children are playing next to the road today." The surprise for an English speaker is slot 4: the noun naming the subject comes late, after the place phrase.

Step 6: unscrambling

Take a practice scramble that is not one of the graded ones: titooa e nakon Meeri te nakonako. Sort the pieces into slots — e is the marker, nakonako the verb, nakon te titooa the place phrase, Meeri the subject, no time word — and you rebuild e nakonako nakon te titooa Meeri, exactly the table sentence "Mary is walking to the store."

Do the same with each A1 scramble: find the person marker (it tells you who the subject is and must agree with the noun in slot 4), pull out the verb, group each preposition with the te/taian phrase that follows it, and put any time expression last. Then translate, remembering that ningaabong forces an English future ("will") while n te bong aei keeps the present.

Step 7: building new sentences (A2)

For an English sentence, work through the slots in order. Ask: who is the subject, and is it singular or plural? That fixes slot 1. Then the verb. Then "next to the store" style phrases go in slot 3 with te or taian as needed. Then the subject noun or pronoun. Then "today" or "tomorrow" at the very end. When the subject is a plural noun, remember the pattern of the table: the noun phrase is enough on its own, but the marker at the front still has to be the plural one.
